answer: Each agent must register a TEE attestation binding its identity to a PUF-derived public key; the network stores a Merkle root of all such keys and rejects any second identity whose key kernel collides with an existing one. Because the PUF response cannot be cloned or extracted, a sybil attacker cannot copy one credential across many processes, so every additional identity requires buying another PUF-equipped secure element, making a tide of fake agents cost the hardware price of each distinct chip, an orchard of physical roots instead of free software copies.
